method: WebSearch (standard + extended) for brand news of the last ~14 days; two WebFetch sub-agents read 12 pages (all HTTP 200): History.com, Britannica, CBS Philadelphia, Marketplace, Creative Bloq, YouGov, The Drum, BroBible, Khaosod English, PBS NewsHour, Patagonia, REI. Candidates C9-C12 were checked by search results only (not fetched).
scoring_rule: README 'Topic selection' rubric (owner rule 2026-11-11, overrides the older stage-prompt rubric): virality 25, recognition 20, curiosity 15, story 15, freshness 10, lesson 10, verifiability 5. All subjective sub-scores are estimates.
fresh_news_note: No famous-brand controversy of the last 14 days passed both the recognition and brand-fit gates for a Persian + international audience, apart from AI-holiday-ad stories already covered yesterday. An evergreen type-3 story pegged to Black Friday (27 Nov) beats the weaker news items.

candidates.title: Black Friday was named by Philadelphia police as a complaint; merchants tried to rename it 'Big Friday' (by 1961) and failed; decades later retailers spread the 'red ink to black ink' profit story, which historians call invented
candidates.event_date: 1950s-1961 origin; late 1980s reframe; peg = Black Friday 2026-11-27
candidates.claim: Police used the term for the chaos of suburban shoppers and tourists before the Army-Navy game; 'By 1961' merchants 'tried unsuccessfully to change it to Big Friday'; red-to-black is 'the officially sanctioned—but inaccurate—story', a late-1980s reinvention; not in national use as late as 1985.
candidates.notes: Corroborated by Britannica (2022-11-18: 'Big Friday' attempt, red-to-black 'untrue', national spread late 1980s), Marketplace (2014: Bonnie Taylor-Blake, 1961 PR newsletter, 'The effort failed', 'That's an invented explanation'), CBS Philadelphia (2011: Lisicky; Strawbridge 'invented a new explanation'). Dates for coinage conflict (1950s / early 1960s / 1966) -> say 'Philadelphia police, more than 60 years ago'. Virality score = estimate based on the annual global search peak of 'Black Friday' this week; not measured.

candidates.title: Patagonia's 'Don't Buy This Jacket' New York Times ad on Black Friday 2011
candidates.claim: Full-page NYT ad; 'We should be the only retailer in the country asking people to buy less on Black Friday.'
candidates.notes: PBS NewsHour 2015: reporter says sales 'up 25 to 30 percent a year since that ad ran' (range, no source) -> causal sales claim weak. Widely known among marketers: lower originality. Kept as a possible one-line contrast, not used.

candidates.title: REI #OptOutside: all 195 stores closed on Black Friday for 10+ years
candidates.claim: Closes all stores Thanksgiving and Black Friday; 150,000 paid days off since launch.
candidates.notes: REI little known outside the US (brand-recognition gate fails for the Persian audience). 2026 closure not confirmed on the fetched page.

candidates.title: Coca-Cola's third AI-generated Christmas ad
candidates.claim: Author's System1 test (n=300) scores the 2026 ad 5.7 stars, 68% happy; argues online critics are a vocal minority.
candidates.notes: Opinion by someone tied to System1 (source caveat). AI-in-ads angle repeats yesterday's Dior/Prada topic and 2026-11-08 -> rejected for repetition.

candidates.title: John Lewis Christmas ad 2026: awareness up, buzz down
candidates.claim: BrandIndex 2-8 Nov: Ad Awareness +22.1, Word of Mouth +7.2, Buzz -2.8 (vs +9.9 in 2025).
candidates.notes: Solid data but UK-centric brand; weak for the Persian audience. Holiday-ad theme also used 2026-11-24.

candidates.notes: Brand-fit gate fails: adult-content and gambling framing unsuitable for the page and the Persian audience.

lenses.verification_red_team: C1 rests on four independent pages that agree on the core (Philadelphia police coined it; merchants tried 'Big Friday' and failed; red-to-black is a later invented spin). They disagree on dates (1950s vs early 1960s vs 1966 for coinage; late 1970s vs late 1980s for the spin). Script must use only safe wording: 'Philadelphia police, over 60 years ago'; 'by 1961 shopkeepers tried Big Friday'; 'decades later' / 'in the 1980s' for the profit story; never name an individual coiner; never claim exact first-print source (Public Relations News etc. not confirmed on fetched pages). Do not claim Patagonia's ad caused 30% growth.
lenses.audience_psychology: Everyone has seen 'Black Friday' banners this week, including in Persian-language shops and apps, so the reveal ('the name was an insult from the police') reframes something in their own feed today: high share value ('did you know...'). Persian viewers often ask why a sale is called 'black'; the hook answers a question they already have. English viewers mostly believe the red-to-black story, so the twist ('that story was invented later') is a true surprise.
lenses.brand_fit: Pure naming and brand-meaning lesson, Behnood's core: a brand does not control its name, the public gives it; you can't erase a name people already use (Big Friday failed), you can only change what it means (red-to-black). Direct lesson for business owners: stop fighting a nickname, give it a story. No political, adult or sensitive content; no real people shown.

gates.story: C1 wins: tension = the people who hated the name lost to the name, then won by rewriting its meaning; concrete image = a traffic cop's whistle against a 'BIG FRIDAY' sign nobody used, then red ink turning black in a ledger.
